articles.title: An Indiana man used a painting to cover a hole in his wall; experts identified it as a Martin Johnson Heade, and Houston’s museum bought it for $1.25 million
articles.summary: An Indiana man used a painting to cover a wall hole, later identified as a rare Martin Johnson Heade masterpiece, which sold for $1.25 million. Discover the story behind this astonishing find.
articles.body: Finding a hidden work of art randomly seems to be the stuff of a treasure hunter’s dream. After all, a fortune does not always come with a certificate of authenticity or hang in a gallery under careful lighting. Sometimes, its value can go unnoticed until someone finally takes a closer look. One such story, almost out of a fantasy, happened when a board game prompted an Indiana homeowner to investigate a painting he had bought with a piece of furniture.The picture had been used to cover a hole in a wall. According to The New York Times, by May 1999, experts had identified it as a flower painting by Martin Johnson Heade, and the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston paid $1.25 million for it.The owner was a tool-and-die-company employee in his thirties and had paid next to nothing for it and the furniture. He liked it but remained clueless about its value. In January 1999, while playing Masterpiece, a board game, he noticed Two Magnolias on Blue Plush, a similar Heade.From a cold email to a museum dealHe went online, found that Kennedy Galleries handled Heade’s work, and emailed the gallery. He asked whether his painting was the work of that artist, then sent digital images of it. The gallery arranged for it to be authenticated and, once done, connected the discovery with the Houston museum. The seller was not identified in the report.The painting titled Magnolias on Gold Velvet Cloth dates to about 1890. Theodore E. Stebbins Jr., author of the1975 catalogue raisonné of Heade’s works, called it an important rediscovery and labelled it a fine example of the artist’s oeuvre. Stebbins, who was also curator of American paintings at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, added it to an updated edition of the catalogue.It was March 1999 when Martha J. Fleischman, president of Kennedy Galleries, told a decorative arts curator at the Museum of Fine Arts that she had made the find of her life, but could not yet say what it was. Emily Ballew Neff, the museum’s curator of American Art, contacted her and wanted to know when she could reveal it. After Fleischman identified the work, Neff immediately knew the museum wanted to acquire it.When the painting arrived for inspection, it remained in its original frame, almost in nearly perfect condition with the original glass protecting its surface. Subsequently, museum director Peter C. Marzio called an emergency meeting of the trustees. They approved the purchase in less than 90 minutes. One anonymous trustee provided most of the money, while two foundations supplied the rest. It was the museum’s first Heade and went on view on 2 June 1999, The New York Times reported. Other Heade flower paintings had also surfaced through sales. In May 1999, Christie’s sold Two Magnolias on Blue Plush for $882,500.How an overlooked artist’s legacy resurfaced Heade was born in Pennsylvania in 1819 and later became known for his landscapes, seascapes, hummingbirds, tropical scenes and flower arrangements. He settled in St. Augustine, Florida, in 1883 and painted many of his floral still lifes there. His magnolia works depict the different stages of blossoms at close range, and fewer than 20 were known, according to The New York Times.Christie’s American paintings expert Paul R. Provost offered one possible explanation for their rediscovery. Based on his assessment, people had bought Heade paintings while holidaying in Florida and taken them home. The works then passed down through families, whose members weren’t always cognisant of the artist’s work. Hence, some remained outside museums and eluded the attention of art specialists.Heade’s reputation had also fluctuated. According to Smithsonian magazine’s 2000 report, despite exhibiting frequently during a 60-year career, he was subjected to critical indifference. For a full four decades after he passed away, his work garnered little notice. An exhibition at New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1944 helped revive interest. Art dealer Robert G. McIntyre saw Heade’s Thunder Storm on Narragansett Bay there and later recalled its artistic force and drama.The Smithsonian report also covered an exhibition organised by Stebbins to present the range of Heade’s work. It was displayed at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston until 17 January 2000, before moving on to the National Gallery of Art in Washington and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jordan sentences three men to death by hanging after deadly church attack
articles.summary: Three men have been convicted of carrying out an attack on a church in the Karak governorate that killed nine people.
articles.body:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out last month’s deadly gun attack on a church in the kingdom’s south.

Gunmen killed nine people and wounded 25 others when they stormed a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan’s Karak governorate on October 23.

Authorities said three men, two Jordanian brothers and their relative by marriage, had fled after the attack and were arrested three days later.

In a statement on Sunday, the Jordanian military said the “State Security Court issued its ruling sentencing to death the three criminals who carried out the terrorist attack” at the church.

The court found them guilty of “committing terrorist attacks” resulting in death, as well as weapons offences, “conspiracy to commit terrorist acts” and “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation”.

“One of the perpetrators of the terrorist operation was also convicted of providing funds with the intention of using them to finance the commission of terrorist acts,” it added.

In late October, Jordanian security forces arrested the three men suspected of the attack that targeted the St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Karak, after clashing with them.

The governorate is home to many members of Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s 11.5 million people.

King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties” as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to attacks after the incident.

articles.title: Bomb threats pose a major question of Europe. But what’s the answer?
articles.summary: An unprecedented wave of bomb threats across Europe has left the bloc struggling to respond, as it remains unclear who is behind the incidents.
articles.body: An unprecedented wave of bomb threats across Europe has left the bloc struggling to respond, as it remains unclear who is behind the incidents. The threats, which are mainly understood to have been sent via emails and have so far all proven false, have impacted multiple media broadcasters, more than 50 flights, thousands of schools and at least one cruise ship across the continent, posing an increasingly urgent security challenge for European authorities. Analysts say the hoaxes have exposed the vulnerability of Europe’s public infrastructure to anonymous and hard-to-trace messages and highlight the bloc’s need for a more coordinated response. The bomb threats targeting European flights were taken seriously by authorities and elicited strong action, which varied between countries. While some authorities diverted flights to other airports, others – such as Hungary and France – scrambled fighter jets to escort the affected passenger planes. Some are calling for European countries to replace fragmented, nation-by-nation reactions with a bloc-wide security framework. The chief executive of budget Hungarian airline Wizz Air, József Váradi, spoke Thursday of the need for more harmonized security procedures and alluded to the possible creation of a central body to manage such hoaxes. He revealed that he had recently held a meeting with European Commission officials to push for a coordinated response. “But this is a very hot potato because of the sovereign nation state concept, and no country wants to concede on this matter, ” Váradi said in a post-earnings call Thursday. ‘Scrambled response’ A threat targeting an airline operating across several countries could involve several law enforcement agencies, meaning that greater information-sharing between countries could prove key to identifying patterns and determining the origin and validity of the threat. Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe, Russia and Eurasia programs at the London-based Chatham House think tank, said that while the initial security responses had been strong, coordination between European countries remains insufficient. At present, each country is responding with “its own toolbox and standards,” due to the threats being a relatively new phenomenon, he told CNN. A first step for improvement, he believes, would be to establish a Europe-wide threat assessment standard. “For instance, emergency measures should depend on corroborating intelligence and the circumstances of each incident at continental level.” He also believes that whoever is behind the attacks is exploiting differences in national procedures. “Europol, national police, in some cases even regional police forces, aviation authorities, all need to compare technical evidence. “So, you have in a way a scrambled response and within that scrambled response you have sub-levels. So, it increases the response time, and it therefore gives more space for anxiety to grow.” The threats also expose that while it is cheap to launch such hoaxes, it is vastly more expensive to counter them. A single email can force a mass security deployment, divert flights or prompt the evacuation of public buildings. Such methods weigh heavily on public resources, cause disruption to daily life and sow public unease. School evacuations One response has been to try to carry on as normal. When thousands of schools in Italy received a threat this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s overarching message to concerned parents was to remain calm and keep disruption to a minimum. Bomb threats were sent via email to around 6,300 Italian schools on Wednesday and around 3,778 on Thursday. While hundreds of schools were evacuated, many also chose to remain open. Meloni proposed new evacuation protocols in the wake of the threats, stipulating that schools should not be evacuated based solely on a mass email and without concrete evidence. Schools in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland also received threatening emails Wednesday. Police warned these were likely hoaxes and education facilities were not evacuated. Meanwhile some UK airports made the decision to remain open despite receiving threats. “As far as the UK is concerned, we’ve seen the airports of Heathrow and Birmingham that managed to continue operating after they received threats, because those were assessed as not credible. So, I think this is something others across Europe could do, rather than saying ‘OK there’s a minor alert, we’ll close everything,’” Roos said. He added, “It matters more than you think, because the moment you evacuate it increases the level of anxiety.” The digital nature of the alerts – the vast majority of them were sent via email – makes it difficult for investigators to track down their origin. While some of them were signed off by certain entities, such as the “Male State,” a Russian ultra-nationalist group, authorities suspect these could be false attributions. Cybersecurity firms Proofpoint and Abnormal Security found a large portion of the threats were sent from legitimate webmail accounts that had been hijacked. Such practices make it difficult for law enforcement to track down those responsible and can keep authorities stuck in a reactive posture. Russia suspicions There are strong suspicions that the incidents could be part of a wider campaign of so-called hybrid warfare, in which hostile actors seek to undermine public confidence and destabilize countries without resorting to conventional military force. European officials have increasingly warned about the threat posed by such tactics, with Russia frequently accused of using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to undermine Western countries. Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in such activities. But French President Emmanuel Macron cautioned against jumping to conclusions over the wave of bomb threats, saying Thursday that there was not yet the evidence to attribute them to foreign powers. “As I speak, we do not have sufficient elements to be able to make an attribution,” Macron told reporters during a meeting of European leaders in Dublin. Roos warned against automatically pointing the finger at Moscow without concrete evidence, saying that this could embolden potential other actors. “We run the risk of empowering, for lack of a better word, many other perpetrators, both state- and non-state actors, if each time there is a threat we immediately attribute it to Moscow without even looking into it,” he said. It also remains unclear whether the threats spanning schools, airlines, broadcasters and other institutions are connected, or whether they originate from a single individual, group or state-backed operation. For now, the challenge is striking the balance between taking every potential threat seriously and ensuring that the anonymous emails do not repeatedly bring essential services to a standstill. As the incidents continue to go beyond national borders, pressure is likely to grow on European governments to establish a more coordinated approach — one that can distinguish credible security threats from attempts to exploit the very precautions designed to protect the public.

articles.title: India pulled 500m people out of poverty. Many of them still barely survive
articles.summary: World Bank says India pulled a record number of citizens out of poverty, but millions of them still live on the edge.
articles.body:
Rajsamand and New Delhi, India – Hema Prajapat, 25, says even “thorns growing inside her stomach” would not hurt as much as hunger does.

By the end of each month, her kitchen shelves are empty; her husband, Hari Prajapat, sinks deeper into debt; and an increasing share of their food supplies is set aside for their nine-year-old son, Divyansh.

But Hema’s family is no longer poor – at least on paper.

She spends 11,000 rupees ($117) a month on her household of three. That is about 49 percent more than the roughly 7,380 rupees ($78) monthly threshold for a family of that size, based on the World Bank’s poverty line.

India, the world’s most populous country, no longer counts its poor. It has not published an official consumption-based poverty estimate in more than a decade. That leaves the World Bank to provide internationally comparable estimates, using newer consumption surveys and its own poverty thresholds.

A recent World Bank report says India lifted nearly 500 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent during the period.

The only comparable poverty-reduction effort on this scale was achieved by China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty over four decades.

Several economists have said India’s achievement is significant, and that the World Bank’s mechanism for calculating these numbers is beyond reproach, even as they have argued that the planet’s most populous nation still has a long way to go before it can claim to have defeated poverty.

Other economists have questioned the World Bank’s sweeping conclusions and India’s unwillingness under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to carry out its own poverty estimates.

But masked by that largely academic and political split is the lived reality of millions of Indians who have crossed the supposed poverty threshold yet lead a life marked by persistent deprivation, and a precarity that leaves families one shock away from losing everything that matters to them.

“This poverty line, this bar, is very low. No person can live a dignified life [on this amount],” Hema told Al Jazeera, sitting in a small garden where she moonlights as a caretaker.

“Did they even get out of their AC cars?” she asked, taking a dig at the officials who prepared the report for the World Bank.

India, home to 1.4 billion people, is one of the fastest-growing global economies – the fourth-largest by nominal gross domestic product (GDP), despite repeated recent shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

It is also one of the world’s most unequal countries, with the top 1 percent of its population owning 40 percent of its wealth – a concern highlighted in the World Bank report as well.

Hema was 11 when she was married off to a man who belongs to a family of traditional clay-pot makers in Rajsamand district of Rajasthan state.

When pot sales could no longer meet their financial needs, her husband, Hari, started a street food stall selling pani puri, a popular Indian snack. That did not last long because of the pandemic.

For the past year, she has been cleaning houses and washing utensils in the neighbourhood for 5,000 rupees ($53) a month, but the deprivation did not end.

“We have to buy every single thing from the market,” she said. The family has no agricultural land.

The World Bank pointed to rising female labour force participation as one of the factors behind India’s improving poverty rates, although women’s access to secure and adequately paid employment remains a challenge.

“Since I started working, our home has seen some comfort, but the money is now vanishing faster, and we are even more in debt,” Hema said, adding that she is unable to figure out the maths behind it.

“The prices have multiplied in recent years, and whatever we earn falls short,” she told Al Jazeera.

The World Bank also noted that the Indian government’s provision of free or subsidised foodgrains to nearly 800 million citizens every month under its national food-security programme has helped tackle extreme poverty.

But a rising cost of living has meant that government subsidies and handouts are racing against growing economic pressures on families like Hema’s. India’s overall consumer prices rose by at least 51 percent between September 2016 and September 2025, according to the government’s Consumer Price Index. Wage rises in this period have not kept pace.

Some government schemes help, such as public schools for children or state-run hospitals that provide free or subsidised healthcare.

But Hema says free healthcare does not inspire much confidence in people. When her son Divyansh had a bad cold and the flu two months ago, she rushed him to a private hospital as waiting times at public hospitals are often longer, with crowded wards, overstretched doctors and limited resources.

“I was scared for him. His fever was getting worse,” she said.

Treatment at the private hospital cost Hema about 6,000 rupees ($64) – more than what she makes in a month. “I do not want my son to get used to private hospitals or their drugs. I cannot take him to one every time,” she said.

Millions of Indian households that appear to be rising above the World Bank’s poverty threshold live on the edge, desperately trying to avoid being pushed back.

Santosh Mehrotra, a developmental economist in New Delhi, said the poverty threshold in India is too low. All it takes is “one shock” to be pushed back into it, he said. “That shock could be a pandemic, drought, flood, or even a wedding.”

Hema’s neighbour Sushila Salvi received one such shock.

In December last year, Salvi, 31, realised she was “finally pregnant” again – her second child after a gap of 14 years. Salvi did not trust government hospitals and wanted to get all her treatment at a private clinic.

In some ways, she had prepared for it. Over the previous eight years, she learned makeup skills and opened a small, one-seater salon in Kankroli, a small town in Rajsamand. She had been saving for her 14-year-old daughter’s higher education. The daughter currently goes to a government school.

“But when I got pregnant, I could not rely on government hospitals,” she said.

Maternal care cost her nearly 65,000 rupees ($695) and drained her savings. She had to pull her daughter out of extra tuition classes that cost her 600 rupees ($6) a month.

Mehrotra, who previously worked with the government on rural economies and poverty, said the World Bank’s poverty threshold is “also problematic because it does not draw a distinction between the rural and the urban populations” despite their different realities.

Seema Kumar, 37, lives on the outskirts of New Delhi and spends 20,000 rupees ($214) on her family of three.

She turns to loans when expenses spiral, such as during a festival or her 17-year-old son’s birthday.

As India celebrated Diwali, a festival of lights, last week, and people burst firecrackers, air quality in New Delhi – one of the world’s most polluted cities – hit a record.

The next morning, as dense and toxic smog hung over the city, all three members of Seema’s family left for work. By evening, her son had developed a sore throat, everyone in the family had a runny nose, and Seema went to bed with a terrible headache.

“I could not buy a mask for my son, and they say I am not poor any more,” Seema told Al Jazeera.

Back in Rajsamand, as Hema swept the garden in her neighbourhood, she called Hari, her husband, reminding him that their child was due for a routine medical checkup that day.

Hari said he could not afford to refill petrol any more due to the increase in oil prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East. Hema offered to refill his motorcycle’s tank to go to the nearest hospital.

“My only hope is that my son makes something out of his life,” said Hema. “If I do not work for a single day – let alone a month – we can go back to the days of extreme poverty and deprivation.”

articles.body: A Florida woman allegedly grabbed her ex-boyfriend’s Pokémon cards during a physical confrontation after realising that the collection was upsetting him, according to police. Nadia Hussain, 23, was arrested in Orlando on November 7 following a dispute at her ex-boyfriend’s apartment. Police said the argument began after he asked her to leave and later escalated into an alleged physical altercation. Hussain is facing charges of domestic battery and witness tampering. The Pokémon cards were not the subject of a theft charge, and police said the collection was not damaged.Florida woman allegedly targeted Pokémon cards after argument with ex-boyfriendAccording to an arrest affidavit cited by Law&Crime, Hussain had spent the night at her ex-boyfriend’s apartment before the two began arguing. He asked her to leave, but she allegedly refused. When he started recording the confrontation and threatened to contact building security, Hussain allegedly knocked his phone from his hand and struck him several times.The argument then turned towards his Pokémon cards, which were lying on a table in the living room. Police said Hussain approached the cards while her ex-boyfriend tried to stop her. She allegedly grabbed them after noticing that doing so affected his behaviour.She allegedly returned to the apartment and tried to reach the cards againThe situation did not end when Hussain initially left the apartment. The Marry Sue reported that she later returned to collect personal belongings, including a bong she had left behind. Her ex-boyfriend allegedly opened the door slightly to hand it to her after she said she would not come inside.According to the police account, Hussain then allegedly forced her way into the apartment and moved towards the living room. Her ex-boyfriend believed she was trying to get to his Pokémon cards again and blocked her path. The two became involved in another physical confrontation, according to the affidavit.Police say Pokémon cards were used to provoke her ex-boyfriendDuring an interview with police, Hussain allegedly said she had been deliberately annoying her ex-boyfriend because she felt he was not showing her enough affection. She also reportedly acknowledged grabbing the Pokémon cards after seeing how much the action affected him.The confrontation became more serious when her ex-boyfriend tried to call 911. Police said Hussain struck his phone several times in an attempt to stop him from making the call. A 911 hang-up was received from his number, and neighbours eventually intervened to help remove Hussain from the apartment.Hussain was arrested and charged with domestic battery and felony witness tampering for allegedly hindering communication with law enforcement, according to Law&Crime. articles.title: What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know
articles.summary: US officials say a routine upgrade that went awry caused the mass disruption of air travel.
articles.body:
Airlines are still scrambling to return operations to normal after the longest and only second nationwide stop of flights in the United States since the attacks of 9/11 in 2001.

More than 5,000 flights were cancelled in the US on Saturday after over 9,000 were scrapped a day earlier as the knock-on effects continued from Friday’s abrupt ground stop . The stoppage was halted after more than four hours on Friday night, but airports and carriers were still grappling with large backlogs and resulting delays.

The decision to suddenly ground all planes on Friday initially triggered speculation of a cyberattack.

But officials have since ruled that out and named the reason for the weekend disruptions as a routine replacement of the communications routers that connect the US air traffic control system.

Here’s everything we know about what went wrong:

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop of flights at 3:54pm East Coast time (20:54 GMT) on Friday, citing a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres.

The outage caused thousands of flights to be cancelled or delayed across the US.

The ground stop was removed at 8:15pm on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday), but hundreds of flights were still delayed or cancelled that night, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop while international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.

A routine upgrade was being carried out – maintenance work that ultimately overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop, US officials said.

L3Harris, a contractor, was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fibre optic lines in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.

The router in that location then started overloading the air traffic control system, causing communications disruptions. When officials couldn’t locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.

“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” Duffy said.

The transportation secretary said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router to start flooding other ones.

“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters.

The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centres.

The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS), a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two routers that were updated on Friday. An official told the Reuters news agency it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas.

An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

Ageing technology and equipment alongside a shortage of several thousand controllers have long been concerns plaguing the US air traffic control system.

Duffy on Friday called for $50bn in funding to upgrade these systems, up from his earlier request of $30bn after Congress approved $12.5bn last year.

White House officials had convened an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday amid concerns that the incident was due to a cyberattack. But the US government has since said it did not believe that was the cause.

“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”

The FAA chief reiterated that view at Saturday’s news conference.

“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.

Who has been named responsible for the incident?

L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company, is the contractor behind the systems upgrade, the US Department of Transportation said.

Three-fourths of the company’s revenue comes from US government contracts, largely from the military, The New York Times reported.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.

“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and safety and reliability are its “highest priorities”.

“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said.

“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

L3Harris said it has been “modernising” the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in “close coordination” with the FAA.

It added that it has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre optic system.

The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any further risks.

When will flights in the US be back to normal?

Bedford, the head of the FAA, cautioned that it could take time.

“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”

He stated that he thinks “the worst is behind us”.

Duffy said airlines were expected to restore their full schedules by Sunday night.

Airlines have issued travel waivers for passengers affected to rebook flights for later dates at no cost.

Tens of thousands of people remain stranded in airports across the country while others have been left to pay surge prices for hotels and rental cars as airlines scramble to resume flights.
